newsitem.title: USA: Female chimps take charge of their lives - study.
newsitem.headline: Female chimps take charge of their lives - study.

text.p: Back in the 1960s, they were thought of as passive vessels who got their status from the rank of the males in their lives. But a new study indicates female chimpanzees have control over their own existence.

The successful female chimp depends more on her rank with other females than she does on her male sex partner's rank, biologists, including famed primatologist Jane Goodall, wrote on Thursday in the current edition of the journal Science.

Drawing on 37 years of observation of chimpanzees at Gombe National Park in Tanzania, the authors found that contrary to former assumptions, patterns of male dominance were not the determining factor in how well females were able to reproduce, one key indicator of success.
In fact, where females ranked in the feminine hierarchy was much more important, co-author Jennifer Williams said in a telephone interview from the University of Minnesota in St. Paul.
"It actually gives you a picture of females who have a lot more control over their own lives," Williams said.
One reason the conclusions took so long to reach was that displays of female dominance were rarer and more subtle than male dominance, she said.

"(Male chimps) use displays which are these big shows of how amazing and wonderful they are; they rattle trees and drag boulders down, things like that ... every day, many times a day," Williams said. "Females might show (signs of dominance) a couple of times a year."
Where male chimpanzees were easy to rank, from top chimp to bottom, scientists could only peg where females placed by ranking them as generally high, middle or low in the hierarchy.

What was clear was that females with high rank -- old or young, large or small -- managed to dominate the choice patches of food and managed to have more progeny in quicker succession than less dominant females. Their young also survived at a higher rate and their daughters matured faster, the scientists found.
Williams said chimp behaviour in this regard might correspond in some ways to human behaviour in adolescence.
Where adolescent boys are often openly obnoxious and will fight with other boys, Williams said, adolescent girls will use different methods to establish status, such as shunning.
Researchers still need to know why female dominance makes such a difference in reproductive success, and what specifically makes one female dominate others, Williams said.
